rows.head: 2bb3616608465da06a22a1a562ed60252bec53e9
rows.commit_message:
Add a how-to page for keeping decision records, and index it. Teams that keep decision records as Markdown files have no record of who accepted one, who reviewed which text, or what replaced it. The page takes a reader from nothing through an adopted, reviewed, merged decision, then a revision and a replacement, and says plainly what colleagues who do not use gitseq still see: the files, the branches, and merge messages that read as the decision log. It is written for someone deciding whether the ceremony is worth it, and assumes no prior reading of the skill or the design note. Every command on the page was run before the page was written, in a throwaway workroom walked end to end, and the docset gate executes all twelve shell blocks on every test run. It documents only what exists today, states that an artifact cannot be ratified and that only the review requester ratifies a verdict, and says ordinary staleness is recorded rather than refused. docs/README.md gains a row for it.

rows.head: 4d5d62b6f2f23d7d3540f3c2ba07abcbea8d6067
rows.commit_message:
Every MCP tool now declares the shape of the structuredContent it already returned.

The adapter has always returned structuredContent while saying nothing about its shape, so a client that decides whether to read it by looking for a declaration had nothing to look at. Each of the fourteen tools now carries an object-typed outputSchema, attached by one loop over the definitions so a tool added later cannot quietly miss it.

The declaration is deliberately permissive: additionalProperties stays true, because no key is present on every return path — each resident-backed tool has a degraded local-fold fallback of a different shape. A wrong schema would be worse than none, since a conformant client validates against it and rejects what does not match. Object is claimed because every success path encodes as an object and object stays readable to older protocol revisions; failures carry no structuredContent at all.

This is conformance and self-description, not the repair of an observed client. The report that prompted the work turned out to involve a client with no structuredContent support whatever, so nothing here claims to have fixed it.

Two tests hold the declaration honest: the schema's type and its permissiveness are each compared against the one admissible value, so any other value fails and names the tool, and real non-empty responses from five tools are validated against their own declared schema.
